Gearhead Got 1970 Mustang Mach 1 in 1984, Raced It, Parked It 35 Years Ago, Never Touched It Since
48 photos
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned
“Presently stored in car trailer and does not run.. It is in need of restoration. Owned since the 1980s. I would rather see an enthusiast bring it back to life than have it continue sitting.” When a gearhead reads these words, the matter is pretty much settled. But when said gearhead is tagged by friends in a comment on the Facebook Marketplace ad for the car, it’s no longer simply car enthusiasm. It’s a mission.
Automotive builder and “Stay Tuned” YouTube channel host Tony Angelo recently abandoned his weekly shop schedule after viewers tagged him in an online listing for a genuine 1970 Ford Mustang Mach 1. Parked for the better part of 35 years, the fastback carries a 351-cubic-inch Cleveland V8 with a 4-speed manual transmission, a Traction-Lok rear axle, factory air conditioning, power steering, and power front disc brakes in a sought-after package.
Located in the Philadelphia area, the Mustang belonged to longtime owner Jeff Miller, who purchased it in 1984 and street-raced it along Front Street before storing it away in the late 1980s or early 1990s. Although the car wore an aging brown repaint over its original gold finish and carried a $16,500 asking price, Angelo arrived the next day with some old photos of dead US presidents, and negotiated. They shook hands at $15,000 for the project.
Considering that restored 1970 Mach 1 models routinely command between $60,000 and $75,000, Angelo viewed the purchase as a compelling bargain despite obvious cosmetic and mechanical neglect. Closer inspection revealed a rusted passenger door skin, a cracked windshield, and localized floor pan corrosion.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Jeff Miller The good news: the structural frame rails, pinch welds, and torque boxes remained remarkably intact, giving the Stay Tuned crew a solid foundation rather than the proverbial basket to carry hopes and prayers.
Back at the shop, Angelo and his team washed away decades of mold and grime before consulting automotive journalist David Freiburger regarding the engine's potential. Jeff had rebuilt the 351 Cleveland prior to parking the car, installing higher-compression TRW pistons, a hot Crane hydraulic camshaft, long-tube headers, and an Accel dual-point mechanical distributor, upgrading the V8 from its factory 300 horsepower rating toward an estimated 400 horsepower on the street.
Reviving an engine dormant for 35 years requires methodical preparation before the first turn of the key. The wrenchers verified that the crankshaft rotated freely, examined the clean cylinder walls and bottom-end bearings with a borescope, and poured equal parts acetone and automatic transmission fluid into each cylinder to free any stuck piston rings before draining the dry oil pan and fabricating a custom drain plug.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned Because roughly 80 percent of internal engine wear occurs during dry startups, Angelo removed the distributor and spun the oil pump shaft counterclockwise until oil pressure reached 75 psi throughout the bearings and valvetrain. Afterward, the team cleaned and gapped the dual ignition points, installed fresh Autolite racing spark plugs gapped to 0.035 inches (0.89 mm), bolted on a new 650-cfm Holley four-barrel carburetor, and restored 12-volt power to the starter solenoid.
When the 351 Cleveland finally coughed to life from a temporary fuel jug, muffled exhaust notes and a shower of acorns revealed that squirrels had packed the mufflers solid over the decades. Angelo promptly sliced the exhaust pipes off behind the long-tube headers, allowing the V8 to idle smoothly (with 18 degrees of ignition advance) and fire all eight cylinders for the first time in more than three decades.
Despite the engine's crisp throttle response , the Mustang remains temporarily immobile inside the garage until its driveline and safety systems are rebuilt. Testing on the lift showed that the transmission had leaked its gear oil, the brake pedal was frozen, the radiator wept coolant, and the clutch assembly refused to engage, leaving Angelo with clear mechanical priorities before taking the revived Mach 1 onto public roads for its maiden drive in the third millennium.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned Cars like Angelo's Philadelphia rescue come from a pivotal moment in Ford's golden-era muscle-car history. Introduced in August 1968 for the 1969 model year, the Mach 1 package transformed the Mustang Sportsroof fastback into an aggressive street machine equipped with competition suspension, matte-black hood paint, locking hood pins, deluxe interior trim, and potent V8 engines.
The Mach 1 was designed to bridge the gap between regular Mustang GTs and costly, limited-production Shelby variants. For 1970, Ford refined the body styling with cleaner single headlights and introduced the legendary 351-cubic-inch Cleveland V8, named after the Ohio foundry where it was cast.
Featuring thin-wall casting, canted valves, and massive cylinder-head ports, the four-barrel M-code Cleveland delivered 300 horsepower at 5,400 rpm with an 11:1 compression ratio as a $48 option, helping Ford sell 40,975 Mach 1 units out of 191,522 total Mustangs built that year.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned The Mach 1 moniker itself originated a decade earlier during the height of Jet Age aerospace ambition, long before the Mustang existed. In a groundbreaking 1959 showcase, Ford stylist Gale Halderman, who later helped pen the original Mustang, co-designed the Ford Levacar Mach 1, a futuristic, wheel-less concept vehicle engineered to glide above specialized rails on a thin cushion of compressed air at speeds approaching the sound barrier (what science refers to as “Mach 1”).
Although the hovercar never reached production, Ford executives retained the evocative aerospace name, applying it to a chopped-roof Mustang concept car in 1967 and 1968 before launching the street-legal Mach 1 for 1969. That inaugural production run achieved instant commercial and motorsport credibility, moving 72,459 cars (some 25% of total Mustang production) in its first year.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned It also set nearly 300 speed and endurance records on Utah's Bonneville Salt Flats and winning national manufacturer rally titles. Over subsequent generations, the Mach 1 nameplate adapted to shifting automotive eras, surviving the 1974 downsizing onto the Mustang II through 1978, returning in 2003 and 2004 with a shaker-hood 4.6-liter V8, and re-emerging from 2021 through 2023 as a 5.0-liter Coyote-powered track-focused coupe.
The 1970 M-code Mach 1 (351C V8 plus 4-speed) was quite rare back in the day, with only 2,937 examples assembled, according to Kevin Marti’s research. For reference, the 428 Cobra Jets came in at 2,501 (both manuals and automatics, though). This particular machine is not a run-of-the-mill ’70 Mustang Mach 1, but a personal challenge for the YouTubing wrencher-rescuer. Promising, but challenge nonetheless.
